A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TANGO, and their main methods, experiments, equations and figures can be reliably matched. However, v1 references supplementary proofs, baseline settings and statistical details that are absent from the supplied PDF; v2 includes Appendices A–C. Comparison of those earlier supplementary details is therefore limited.

before.justification: v1 reports original clustering experiments on four synthetic and 16 real-world datasets, parameter-sensitivity tests and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and reports additional image-segmentation results, running times, noisy-data evaluations and a failure example.

M1.justification: v2 Algorithm 3 revises the path-similarity computation to operate on modes and inter-subcluster edges, replacing the point-level connected-component processing in v1 Algorithm 2. This refines one computational component; the typicality equations, dependency-breaking rule, path-similarity definition and final spectral clustering remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The original four synthetic and 16 real-world datasets remain. v2 adds pixel-level segmentation of six Berkeley benchmark images, extending coverage beyond clustering the existing feature datasets. Appendix C.7 also introduces highly noisy irregular-shape datasets and an extreme-density-contrast test scenario.

E2.justification: The corresponding original experiments retain their comparator sets: ten real-world baselines and Quick Shift/DPC for the synthetic examples. The added segmentation experiment reuses QKSPP, CPF, LDP-MST and LDP-SC; no new external comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: The original normalization, 64-dimensional image representations, metrics and TANGO parameter search remain. The added segmentation protocol uses 154,401 five-dimensional position/RGB vectors per image, fixed parameters and runtime measurements. Appendix C.6 also changes the TANGO-c control from replacing the similarity weighting to removing aggregation.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the original similarity-weighting ablation with an aggregation-removal ablation and corresponding results. It also adds a controlled illustration of typicality as points are added (Figure 3), noisy-data tests (Figure 11) and a concrete failure case (Figure 12). The original neighborhood-size sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report Friedman testing followed by Nemenyi comparisons with CD = 2.30. v2 supplies the statistic, exact p-value and pairwise rank differences for these already reported tests, without introducing a new statistical procedure. Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores are unchanged between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 5. v2 adds segmentation outcomes and timings, noisy-data findings, detailed statistical outputs and replacement TANGO-c results. It also introduces an unresolved discrepancy: Table 2 gives TANGO banknote ARI/NMI/ACC as 96.53/93.59/99.13, while both benchmark figures report 96.24/93.17/99.05.

T1.justification: The uniqueness and linear-time typicality theorems are retained and now have proofs in the supplied material. v2 adds Theorem 3 and Appendix A.2 claiming an O(nk log(nk)) path-similarity bound, replacing v1's O(n^2 log n) analysis. Appendix B additionally introduces a stochastic recurrence, independence and degree-distribution assumptions, and a power-law tail theorem.

C1.justification: The central claims about global typicality, mode identification and graph-cut clustering remain. v2's introduction explicitly adds characterization of typicality's statistical properties to the contributions, extending the earlier claims about uniqueness and computational efficiency.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the Katz-centrality comparison with a PageRank/attraction-basin interpretation and expands explanations of mode selection, aggregation and stability as k increases. It adds substantive qualifications: segmentation results are preliminary and imperfect, and typicality can fail when sparse points surround a much denser core.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's references to unavailable supplementary settings, v2 supplies baseline search grids, manual-selection procedures and per-dataset parameter values in Appendix C and Table 2. It also adds code-access information and the segmentation hardware, software and 20-thread similarity-computation setting. These disclosures do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial spectral-clustering review covering guarantees, scalable methods and cluster-number selection. It removes the Katz-centrality positioning and introduces PageRank and power-law literature to motivate and analyze typicality, substantially expanding the work's connections to prior research.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten around confidence in mode identification. v2 adds a preliminaries section and reorganizes detailed results, sensitivity analysis and ablations into Appendix C, substantially changing the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration and adds a workflow diagram, typicality-evolution plot, detailed results/parameter table, statistical heatmap, segmentation grid, noise examples and failure visualization. Existing diagnostic plots are relocated and enlarged in the appendix. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical edits.

improvement.justification: For the supplied PDFs, v2 substantially improves completeness and assessability: central proofs and experimental settings previously deferred to unavailable material are now inspectable, while clearer explanations and a concrete failure case improve understanding of the method's scope. Segmentation timings and noise tests extend its empirical support. The gains are tempered by inconsistent banknote scores and insufficient justification that Appendix B's distributional assumptions apply to the evaluated data.
